This report describes how survey responses were prepared and scored, how the
resulting measures relate to one another, and how those measures relate to
author recognition performance. It is organized to make the study's findings
and scoring decisions accessible for manuscript writing.

# 1. Cleaning the data and defining the sample

The raw survey exports were checked for incomplete records, duplicate
submissions, and straight-line response patterns. Duplicate attempts were
reviewed and resolved by retaining the most complete, usable submission.
Flagged participant records were also manually reviewed against the survey
audit materials, including recordings, before final inclusion decisions.
Practice and test records were excluded. These steps produced a final analysis
sample of **82 participants**, each with complete, usable data from all four
administered surveys.

One of the 82 participants gave a straight-line response to the survey's
question about AI-tool use. That response is omitted only from analyses of
that survey question; all other analyses use the full 82-person sample.

Participants completed one writing session alone and one with an LLM, in
counterbalanced order. The IMI and writing self-efficacy survey (WSE) followed
the writing-alone session; Beliefs about AI and AI Reflection followed the
LLM session.

# 2. How survey responses become scores

We use the published scoring structure for each survey, noting how that
structure was developed and supported. The IMI has long-standing subscales;
Chan and Zhou’s Beliefs about AI groups were theory-led and evaluated with
CFA; WSE uses groupings recommended from the source study’s exploratory
analysis. Scores are item means, so they remain on the response scale and are
straightforward to interpret.

## 2.1 Previously published scoring approaches

Chan and Zhou developed their Beliefs about AI items from Expectancy-Value
Theory and organized them into four broad sections: Knowledge (5 items),
Perceived Value (11), Perceived Cost (4), and Intention (2). They divided
Perceived Value into Attainment (items 7–10), Intrinsic (11–13), and Utility
(14–17), reflecting different reasons a behavior may be valued: importance,
enjoyment, and practical usefulness. Their analyses tested the Knowledge,
full Value, and Cost item groups with separate confirmatory factor models; the
three facets are subdivisions of the Value items. We follow those item
groupings. Because the facets overlap strongly in our sample, we foreground
the full Value score and show the facets as supporting detail.

The IMI uses its established Interest/Enjoyment, Perceived Competence, and
Effort/Importance subscales. We apply those published item groupings and score
each subscale as its item mean.

For writing self-efficacy (WSE), we use the item groupings recommended in the
PSWSES paper; we treat these as source-recommended scoring groups rather than
established subscales. The authors used principal-components analysis with varimax
rotation in a sample of 505 students, then reviewed the groups with writing
experts. Their three recommended groupings are Local/Global Writing Process
Knowledge, Physical Reaction, and Time/Effort. We applied the authors'
subsequent item reassignment: item 10 to Time/Effort and items 13 and 15 to
Local/Global Writing Process Knowledge; item 3 remains in both Process and
Time/Effort as in the source. The paper found its original item 19 did not
load clearly and suggested replacing it; our survey includes the proposed
writing-resources replacement, which we assign to Time/Effort. In our sample,
the group means have alpha values of .89, .74, and .61, respectively (see
Section 3). The five response points (0, 25, 50, 75, 100) are expressed on a
1–5 scale.

Reverse-worded IMI statements (items 3, 4, 13, 15, and 18) are already
oriented in the supplied survey data. Beliefs about AI cost statements
(items 17–20) are also supplied in reverse-coded form; we flip them back so
that higher scores consistently mean greater perceived cost. These are the
items that are reverse-coded for the reported scores.

## 2.2 AI Reflection: a study-specific grouping

AI Reflection was written for this study and has no published subscales. We
use the two groups from our exploratory analysis: **Enjoyment & Satisfaction**
(items 1–3) and **Ownership & Usefulness** (items 4–12). These labels reflect
the content of the statements in each group. We score each group as the mean
of its items.

# 3. The scores

Each score is the **mean of its listed item responses**. “No. of items” is the
number of statements averaged; “Items averaged” lists their item numbers.
Some source-recommended groups intentionally share an item. “Mean (SD)” gives
the participants' average score and its spread. “Cronbach's alpha” summarizes
internal consistency for the group. Primary measures are emphasized in the
main results; additional scores provide facets or overall summaries.

```{r scorecard}
score_purpose <- tribble(
  ~scale, ~purpose,
  "b_knowledge", "Self-rated understanding of AI limits",
  "b_value", "Perceived value and usefulness of AI",
  "b_cost", "Perceived costs and concerns about AI",
  "b_intention", "Intention to integrate AI",
  "b_attainment", "Attainment value facet (supporting detail)",
  "b_intrinsic", "Intrinsic value facet (supporting detail)",
  "b_utility", "Utility value facet (supporting detail)",
  "i_interest", "Interest and enjoyment",
  "i_competence", "Perceived competence",
  "i_effort", "Effort and importance",
  "w_total", "Overall writing self-efficacy (supporting summary)",
  "w_process", "Local/Global Writing Process Knowledge",
  "w_physical", "Physical Reaction",
  "w_timeeffort", "Time/Effort",
  "a_process", "Enjoyment & Satisfaction",
  "a_product", "Ownership & Usefulness",
  "a_total", "Overall AI Reflection mean (supporting summary)"
)
desc |>
  left_join(manifest |> select(scale, display_label, tier, items), by = "scale") |>
  left_join(score_purpose, by = "scale") |>
  arrange(desc(tier == "headline"), match(instrument, c("Beliefs", "IMI", "WSE", "AIRef"))) |>
  transmute(Priority = if_else(tier == "headline", "Primary measure", "Additional score"),
            Survey = instrument, Score = display_label, Meaning = purpose,
            `No. of items` = str_count(items, ",") + 1L,
            `Items averaged` = str_replace_all(items, ",", ", "),
            `Mean (SD)` = paste0(f2(mean), " (", f2(sd), ")"),
            `Cronbach's alpha` = f2(alpha)) |>
  show()
```

Choose a survey to see the item statements for its scores. The table defaults

# 4. Correlations among survey measures

Every cell is a Spearman correlation between two **item-means** (not factor
scores). Labels mix published item groupings (Beliefs, IMI, and WSE) and the
two groups from the AI Reflection exploratory analysis. Axis labels already
prefix the survey. Caption on the figure: n = `r n_main`.

![](funnel_out/plots/Survey_Measure_Correlations.png)

All displayed pairs are tested. Stars show associations that survive
Benjamini–Hochberg (*) or Bonferroni (**) correction across the primary
measure pairs. The plot reports Spearman correlations between item means.

Between-survey primary measure pairs that survive Benjamini–Hochberg
correction, sorted by rho. Within-survey pairs remain tested and visible in
the correlation map above.

```{r family-b-bars, fig.width = 13, fig.height = 8}
b_hits <- findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "B:"), survives_bh,
         survey_of[predictor] != survey_of[outcome]) |>
  mutate(pair = paste0(lab_s[predictor], "\n× ", lab_s[outcome]),
         pair = factor(pair, levels = pair[order(estimate)]),
         star = if_else(survives_bonf, "**", "*"))
ggplot(b_hits, aes(estimate, pair, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star),
                hjust = if_else(estimate >= 0, -0.15, 1.15)), size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8",
                       midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.55, 0.85),
                     breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.6, 0.2),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rho", y = NULL,
       title = "Cross-survey primary measure associations",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; * survives Benjamini–Hochberg; ** survives Bonferroni correction")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8, lineheight = 0.95),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 18, 14, 18))
```

## Comparison with Chan & Zhou (Pearson r with Intention)

```{r family-a}
src <- c(b_knowledge = .179, b_value = .603, b_attainment = .587,
         b_intrinsic = .456, b_utility = .502, b_cost = -.301)
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "A:")) |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[predictor],
            `This sample` = f2(estimate),
            `Chan & Zhou (N = 405)` = f2(src[predictor]), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2)) |>
  show()
```

n = `r n_main` here.

Value, its facets, and Cost replicate in direction and size. Knowledge runs
the opposite way, likely helped by its ceiling; treat it as a divergence.

# 5. Author Recognition Test

**Author recognition score** = number of real authors recognized minus number of fake-author
foils endorsed. It indexes prior print exposure, not an outcome of the AI
session. False alarms are rare
(`r round(100 * mean(scores$art_fake_false_alarms == 0))`% of participants
picked none), so hits and net are nearly the same number.

```{r art-table}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "D:")) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[predictor], `Correlation with author recognition` = f2(estimate),
            `95% CI` = paste0(f2(ci_low), " to ", f2(ci_high)),
            `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Verdict = verdict) |>
  show()
```

```{r art-heatmap, fig.width = 6.2, fig.height = 5.2}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "D:")) |>
  mutate(score = factor(lab_s[predictor], levels = rev(lab_s[primary_order])),
         star = case_when(survives_bonf ~ "**", survives_bh ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")) |>
  ggplot(aes("Author recognition\n(real − false alarms)", score, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star)), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman\nrho") +
  labs(x = "Author recognition score (real authors − false alarms)", y = "Survey measure",
       title = "Survey measures and author recognition",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; * survives BH; ** survives Bonferroni (",
                         sum(manifest$tier == "headline"), " tests)")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The old scatter plots and their new versions are compared in
`explain/ART_Old_vs_New.png`.

People who recognize more authors hold less positive views of AI and rate
the AI summary's ownership and usefulness lower. These are bivariate
associations; they do not establish confounding.

# 6. Design checks: order and article topic

Question: do **average primary measure scores** depend on which session came first,
or on which article topic that survey followed?

Method: for each of the 12 primary measures, a Type II ANOVA with
`session order × article topic`. Topic is the article for the session that
survey followed (Beliefs and AI Reflection → AI session topic; IMI and WSE →
writing-alone topic). BH is applied within each term across the 12 scores. The
WSE reporting-priority change followed initial results, so its score-level
checks are exploratory rather than prespecified.
Tool (AI vs alone) cannot be tested: each survey was given after only one
session type.

```{r design-checks}
dc <- rd("15_design_checks_order_topic.csv")
dc |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[score], Term = term, F = f2(f), p = signif(p, 2),
            `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2),
            Verdict = if_else(survives_bh, "survives BH", "ns")) |>
  show()
```

```{r design-checks-note, results='asis'}
topic_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "topic", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
order_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "order", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
ix_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "order_x_topic", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
if (length(topic_hit) + length(order_hit) + length(ix_hit) == 0) {
  cat("No order, topic, or interaction term survives BH. Mean scores do not depend on which session came first or which article people got.\n")
} else {
  if (length(order_hit)) cat("Order survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[order_hit], collapse = ", "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  if (length(ix_hit)) cat("Order × topic survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[ix_hit], collapse = ", "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  if (length(topic_hit)) {
    cat("**Topic** survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[topic_hit], collapse = ", "),
        ". That means mean levels of those scores differ by article. ",
        "The table below re-checks associations involving those measures as **partial Spearman** ",
        "correlations controlling for topic (raw rho vs topic-controlled rho).\n\n",
        sep = "")
    if (file.exists(file.path(out, "15b_topic_partial_correlations.csv"))) {
      print(rd("15b_topic_partial_correlations.csv") |>
        transmute(`Pair involving topic-hit score` = paste(lab_s[predictor], "×",
                    if_else(outcome %in% names(lab_s), lab_s[outcome], outcome)),
                  `Raw rho` = f2(raw_rho), `Partial rho (topic controlled)` = f2(estimate),
                  `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2),
                  Verdict = if_else(survives_bh, "survives BH", "ns")) |>
        knitr::kable())
    }
  }
}
```

# 7. AI-tool use

n = `r q17_n` (one of the `r n_main` analysis participants is dropped for a
straight-line response to the AI-tool use survey).

**Why ChatGPT as the main tool score.** Among the `r q17_n` usable responses to the AI-tool use survey,
ChatGPT is by far the most-used AI tool on the checklist (rated 3+ "rarely"
or more). Grammarly is common too but is an editor, so it is excluded from
breadth. The two reported AI-tool use scores are: ChatGPT frequency (single 1–5 item)
and breadth (count of other tools rated 3+, Grammarly excluded). Means across
all tools, bucket proportions, and "primary model" groups are not used.

```{r q17-why-setup}
q17_long <- read_csv("09_q17_ai_use/csv/Q17_Responses_Long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(participant_id %in% scores$participant_id, !is.na(use_score))
chatgpt_tool <- "ChatGPT (including DALL-E) by OpenAI"
tool_use <- q17_long |>
  summarise(pct_use = mean(use_score >= 3) * 100, mean_score = mean(use_score),
            .by = tool) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_use))
chat_row <- tool_use |> filter(tool == chatgpt_tool)
n_use_chat <- sum(q17_long$tool == chatgpt_tool & q17_long$use_score >= 3)
q17_wide <- q17_long |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = participant_id, names_from = tool, values_from = use_score)
gram_cols <- grep("Grammarly", names(q17_wide), value = TRUE)
ai_wide <- q17_wide |> select(-participant_id, -any_of(gram_cols))
chat_v <- ai_wide[[chatgpt_tool]]
other_max <- ai_wide |> select(-all_of(chatgpt_tool)) |> apply(1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
pct_sole <- mean(chat_v > other_max) * 100
pct_tied <- mean(chat_v >= other_max) * 100
gemini_pct <- tool_use$pct_use[tool_use$tool == "Gemini (formerly Bard) by Google"]
```

ChatGPT: `r round(chat_row$pct_use)`% (`r n_use_chat`/`r q17_n`) rated 3+; mean
`r f2(chat_row$mean_score)`. Next AI tool (Gemini): `r round(gemini_pct)`%.
ChatGPT is sole highest-rated AI tool for `r round(pct_sole)`% of participants
and tied-or-highest for `r round(pct_tied)`%.

```{r q17-why-plot, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.5}
tool_labels <- c(
  "ChatGPT (including DALL-E) by OpenAI" = "ChatGPT (OpenAI, incl. DALL-E)",
  "Grammarly" = "Grammarly",
  "Gemini (formerly Bard) by Google" = "Gemini (Google, formerly Bard)",
  "Claude by Anthropic" = "Claude (Anthropic)",
  "Duck Duck Go AI Chat" = "DuckDuckGo AI Chat",
  "Copilot (Bing Chat) by Microsoft" = "Copilot / Bing Chat (Microsoft)",
  "DeepSeek" = "DeepSeek",
  "Meta AI (Facebook)" = "Meta AI (Facebook)",
  "GitHub Copilot" = "GitHub Copilot"
)
tool_use |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(label = unname(coalesce(tool_labels[tool], tool)),
         label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct_use, label, fill = tool == chatgpt_tool)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct_use)), hjust = -0.12, size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#3b73a8", `FALSE` = "#b0b7be"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 110), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "% rating tool 3+ (rarely or more)", y = NULL,
       title = "Most-used AI tools",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", q17_n, "; ChatGPT highlighted")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

```{r q17-table}
q17_lab <- c(q17_chatgpt = "ChatGPT frequency (1–5)", q17_breadth = "Breadth (ex Grammarly)")
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "Q:")) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(`AI-tool use score` = q17_lab[predictor], Score = lab_s[outcome], rho = f2(estimate),
            `95% CI` = paste0(f2(ci_low), " to ", f2(ci_high)),

```

```{r q17-heatmap, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 5}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "Q:")) |>
  mutate(q17 = factor(q17_lab[predictor], levels = q17_lab),
         score = factor(lab_s[outcome], levels = rev(lab_s[primary_order])),
         star = case_when(survives_bonf ~ "**", survives_bh ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")) |>
  ggplot(aes(q17, score, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman\nrho") +
  labs(x = "AI-tool use score", y = "Survey measure",
       title = "AI-tool use and survey measures",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", q17_n, "; * survives BH; ** survives Bonferroni (20 tests)")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

ChatGPT × Intention is mostly a validity check: people who already use
ChatGPT say they intend to keep using AI. Breadth asks whether using more
tools beyond ChatGPT lines up with the same scores.

# 8. Item-level reading lists

Full-sample item scans (n = `r n_main`), shown before the order-split section
because splitting by session order roughly halves n.

Ranking: Bonferroni survivors first, then BH-only, then the rest; within
each, cross-session pairs first, then by |rho|. Corrections are within each
family; order only aids reading. (R) marks reverse-scored IMI items. Only
survivors are shown; full lists:
`funnel_out/10_item_x_score_ranked.csv` and `11_item_x_item_ranked.csv`.

## Item-level associations with primary measures

```{r item-score-bars, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
# Axis uses item IDs only; full wording is in the table under the plot.
# Bars sorted by |rho| for reading; rank number still matches the table order.
ixs <- rd("10_item_x_score_ranked.csv") |> filter(evidence != "not significant")
ixs_top <- ixs |>
  arrange(reading_rank) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  arrange(rho) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("#", reading_rank, "  ", score, "  ×  ", item_id(item)),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label)),
         star = if_else(str_detect(evidence, "Bonferroni"), "**", "*"))
ggplot(ixs_top, aes(rho, label, fill = rho)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(rho), star),
                hjust = if_else(rho >= 0, -0.12, 1.12)), size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8",
                       midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(min(0, min(ixs_top$rho) - 0.05),
                                max(ixs_top$rho) + 0.12),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rho", y = NULL,
       title = "Top 20 item–measure associations",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; sorted by rho; # = reading-list rank; full wording in table; * BH; ** Bonferroni")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

```{r item-score}
ixs |>
  transmute(Rank = reading_rank, Evidence = evidence, Sessions = session_relation,
            Score = score, Item = item, rho = f2(rho), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2)) |>
  long_table()
```

## Items x items

```{r item-item-bars, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
ixi <- rd("11_item_x_item_ranked.csv") |> filter(evidence != "not significant")
ixi_top <- ixi |>
  arrange(reading_rank) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  arrange(rho) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("#", reading_rank, "  ", item_id(item_a), "  ×  ", item_id(item_b)),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label)),
         star = if_else(str_detect(evidence, "Bonferroni"), "**", "*"))
ggplot(ixi_top, aes(rho, label, fill = rho)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(rho), star),
                hjust = if_else(rho >= 0, -0.12, 1.12)), size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8",
                       midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(min(0, min(ixi_top$rho) - 0.05),
                                max(ixi_top$rho) + 0.12),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rho", y = NULL,
       title = "Top 20 item × item hits",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; sorted by rho; # = reading-list rank; full wording in table; * BH; ** Bonferroni")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

```{r item-item}
ixi |>
  transmute(Rank = reading_rank, Evidence = evidence, Sessions = session_relation,
            `Item A` = item_a, `Item B` = item_b, rho = f2(rho), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2)) |>
  long_table()
```

Most item-level hits come from items answered in the same sitting (Beliefs ×
AI Reflection; IMI × WSE). Some of that may be shared mood or response style
within one survey.

# 9. Session order (does a correlation change?)

Placed last among the main sections: splitting by session order roughly
halves n (`r sum(scores$sess_order == "Traditional_First")` Traditional_First,
`r sum(scores$sess_order == "AI_First")` AI_First).

Question: does a correlation change depending on which session came first?
Each correlation is computed separately in the two order groups and compared
with Fisher's z (Spearman variance factor 1.06).

```{r order-scores}
o12 <- rd("12_order_score_x_score_ranked.csv")
o12 |>
  filter(evidence != "not significant" | reading_rank <= 5) |>
  transmute(`Score A` = a_label, `Score B` = b_label,
            `Traditional first` = f2(rho_traditional_first), `AI first` = f2(rho_ai_first),
            Pooled = f2(rho_pooled), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Evidence = evidence, Pattern = pattern) |>
  show()
```

Nearly every surviving order effect involves IMI Interest/Enjoyment with AI
attitudes. When writing alone came first, people who enjoyed it more held
less positive AI views; when AI came first, the relationship reversed.
Pooled, it looks like zero. Groups are small, levels share people and items,
and the pattern was noticed before this test was run — treat as a lead for a
planned model, not a finding.

Item-level order effects that survive correction:

```{r order-items}
bind_rows(
  rd("13_order_item_x_score_ranked.csv") |> mutate(Level = "item x score"),
  rd("14_order_item_x_item_ranked.csv") |> mutate(Level = "item x item")
) |>
  filter(evidence != "not significant") |>
  transmute(Level, A = a_label, B = b_label,
            `Traditional first` = f2(rho_traditional_first), `AI first` = f2(rho_ai_first),
            Pooled = f2(rho_pooled), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Evidence = evidence) |>
  long_table()
```

# Appendix A. Additional measure correlations

![](funnel_out/plots/All_Survey_Measure_Correlations.png)

Includes the three value facets, the overall WSE mean, and the AI Reflection
total (all still item-means). All displayed pairs are tested; stars indicate
associations that survive correction within the primary or additional measure
group. Within-survey correlations involving an overall total and one of its
components are excluded because they overlap by construction.

Does any additional measure show associations that differ from those for the
primary measures? Each surviving additional-score correlation is listed next
to a related primary-measure association where one exists. The overall WSE
mean and AI Reflection total each combine multiple dimensions and therefore
have no single counterpart.

```{r detail-check}
parent <- c(b_attainment = "b_value", b_intrinsic = "b_value", b_utility = "b_value")
up <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% names(parent), parent[x], x)
headline_hits <- findings |> filter(startsWith(family, "B:") | startsWith(family, "D:"))
key <- function(a, b) paste(pmin(a, b), pmax(a, b))
findings |>
  filter((startsWith(family, "C:") | startsWith(family, "D2:")) & survives_bh) |>
  mutate(ha = up(predictor), hb = up(outcome),
         hit = match(key(ha, hb), key(headline_hits$predictor, headline_hits$outcome)),
         counterpart = case_when(
           !is.na(hit) ~ paste0(lab[ha], " x ", lab[hb], ": ", f2(headline_hits$estimate[hit]),
                                " (", headline_hits$verdict[hit], ")"),
           ha == "w_total" | hb == "w_total" ~ "no single counterpart (overall WSE mean)",
           TRUE ~ "no single counterpart (AI Reflection total)")) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(`Additional score pair` = paste(lab[predictor], "x", lab[outcome]), rho = f2(estimate),
            Verdict = verdict, `Related primary association` = counterpart) |>
  long_table()
```

The WSE total-score comparison is retained as additional context; it does not
map to any one WSE group. Read it alongside the three primary WSE group
associations and the scoring limitations above.
